html:
The Battle of Lützen was fought on 16 November 1632 near the town of Lützen, southwest of Leipzig in Saxony, eastern Germany. The Swedish army beat the emperor's army under Albrecht von Wallenstein, but the Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus was killed.

After his victory at Breitenfeld, Gustavus had overrun much of Germany. The emperor called back Wallenstein, his best general, who checked the Swedes in the south and then invaded Saxony, their ally. In November Wallenstein thought the fighting season was over and began to spread his men into winter quarters. Gustavus saw his chance and attacked, with about 19,000 men on each side. Morning fog delayed the start and gave Wallenstein time to dig in along a road and recall his cavalry. Gustavus rode into the enemy while leading a cavalry charge and was shot dead. The Swedes pressed on and took the emperor's guns by dark. Wallenstein retreated in the night.

Sweden had won the field and saved Saxony, but had lost the leader of the Protestant cause. Its chancellor Oxenstierna kept the army in Germany. The Thirty Years' War dragged on for sixteen more years, to the Peace of Westphalia.
